```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
```

A survey tow that catches no fish and a tow that catches a large biomass tell
us different things about habitat. Does depth affect the chance of encountering
Pacific cod, the density when cod are caught, or both? Can a depth curve explain
the geographical patterns in these observations?

This article uses gratia to examine those questions after fitting a spatial
model with sdmTMB. The smooth extraction and effect plots are new gratia methods
for sdmTMB models. The diagnostics also use the spatial and temporal fields in
the complete model. See [Checking a fitted model](model-checking.html) for shared
ideas about residuals, dependence and posterior predictive checks.

## Data and a model for two parts of the survey response

We adapt the Pacific cod survey examples in sdmTMB's
[introduction](https://sdmtmb.github.io/sdmTMB/articles/basic-intro.html) and
[delta-model article](https://sdmtmb.github.io/sdmTMB/articles/delta-models.html).
The data are trawl tows in Queen Charlotte Sound, British Columbia. Biomass
density is measured in kg/km²; `X` and `Y` are UTM coordinates in kilometres.
We retain all survey years and the spatial and year-specific fields. Our
adaptations add a separate mean for each survey year, use six basis functions
for the depth smooth, and use the introduction's 10 km mesh cutoff.

You need the optional package **sdmTMB >= 1.2.0** and models fitted with its
RTMB backend, which is the default. Refit older models or TMB fits with
`control = sdmTMBcontrol(backend = "rtmb")`. mgcv supplies the smooth
syntax. The example also uses dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2 and patchwork. Fitting and simulation
cost more than plotting an ordinary GAM, so we use modest simulation counts.

```{r packages}
library("sdmTMB")
library("mgcv")
library("gratia")
library("dplyr")
library("ggplot2")
library("patchwork")

set.seed(1401)
cod <- pcod
cod$year_f <- factor(cod$year)
cod |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(tows = n(), proportion_zero = mean(density == 0),
    mean_density = mean(density), .groups = "drop")
```

The zero proportions and means vary between years. A mean calculated from the
observed tows is also influenced by where those tows occurred; it is not an
area-standardised biomass index.

```{r observed-cod, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Observed Pacific cod density at survey tows, separated by year."}
ggplot(cod, aes(X, Y, colour = density)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol = 4) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(transform = "log1p", breaks = c(0, 10, 100, 1000, 5000)) +
  labs(x = "Easting (km)", y = "Northing (km)",
    colour = "Density (kg/km²)")
```

The colour scale uses `log1p`, the logarithm of one plus density, to distinguish
the many smaller catches while retaining zeros and the largest catches.
There are many exact zeros and a long positive tail. A Gaussian response model
would allow negative density and impose constant response variance. A Tweedie
model is one useful alternative for zeros plus continuous positive values.
Here a **delta-Gamma model** makes the encounter and positive-density questions
explicit. Its first component models whether density is positive using a logit
link; its second models positive density using a Gamma distribution and log
link. Thus

\[
 E(Y_i) = \Pr(Y_i > 0)\,E(Y_i\mid Y_i>0).
\]

Depth need not have the same effect on both components. Each has its own smooth
coefficients and spatial fields. A persistent field represents geographical
variation shared across survey years; an independent field for each survey year
represents additional geographical variation in that year. These fields allow
nearby tows to share unexplained variation. We choose independent year fields
because this survey did not run every year. An AR1 model would require an
explicit decision about missing time steps and assumptions about correlation
between years.

```{r fit-cod}
cod_mesh <- make_mesh(cod, c("X", "Y"), cutoff = 10)
cod_fit <- sdmTMB(
  density ~ year_f + s(depth, k = 6),
  data = cod, mesh = cod_mesh, time = "year",
  spatial = "on", spatiotemporal = "iid", family = delta_gamma()
)
sanity(cod_fit)
```

The factor accounts for changes in average encounter probability and positive
catch density between surveys. It prevents the year-specific fields from being
the only way to represent a change in the overall mean. Both components use
the same formula and smooth basis, as required by sdmTMB for delta models with
smooths, but their fitted curves can differ. Smoothing is estimated during
fitting. `sanity()` checks estimation and convergence. The fitted positive-density
field has a range of about 12 km, close to the 10 km mesh cutoff, so compare a
finer mesh before relying on its geographical predictions. The residual checks
below examine the response distribution and remaining spatial patterns.

## Which part of the response changes with depth?

```{r smooth-names}
smooths(cod_fit)
```

`s(depth)` belongs to the encounter component and `s.1(depth)` to the positive
component. The `.1` suffix identifies the second predictor.

```{r cod-depth-effects, fig.alt = "Estimated depth smooths for encounter log odds and log positive density, with uncertainty bands and component subtitles."}
depth_panels <- draw(cod_fit, select = smooths(cod_fit), n = 100,
  wrap = FALSE)
(depth_panels[[1]] + labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Contribution to log odds")) |
  (depth_panels[[2]] + labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Contribution to log density"))
```

The first curve is a contribution to **log odds of encounter**, the second to
**log mean positive density**. In this fit both curves peak near 140--150 m.
The encounter curve falls especially sharply in deeper water. The positive
component also favours intermediate depths, but its vertical scale and units
differ; compare shapes within each panel rather than comparing heights across
panels. Few observations support the deepest part of the fitted range, as the
rugs show.

These are partial effects. They omit intercepts, survey-year effects and
spatial fields, so their heights are not encounter probabilities or predicted
densities. `fun = exp` would exponentiate a partial effect, not create a full
prediction. The bands use the joint fitted covariance, retaining the effect of
spatial modelling on coefficient uncertainty. By default, smooth bands also
include uncertainty in the component's overall mean. They are pointwise bands,
not a simultaneous claim about the entire curve. Use `overall_uncertainty =
FALSE` for uncertainty in the term alone.

For your own plots or calculations, retain the estimates rather than extracting
values from the figure:

```{r cod-smooth-table}
depth_effects <- smooth_estimates(cod_fit, n = 100, interval = "confidence")
depth_effects |>
  group_by(.smooth, .model) |>
  slice_max(.estimate, n = 1) |>
  select(.smooth, .model, depth, .estimate, .se)
```

The reported peak depths locate the maxima on the 100-point evaluation grid.
The broad intervals in deeper water reflect sparse observations there, so the
intermediate-depth peak is better supported than the shape of the deep-water
tail.

`smooth_coefs()` returns coefficients in the constrained mgcv basis. They can
be useful for reproducing a curve from its basis matrix, but individual
coefficients do not have the interpretation of a linear depth slope:

```{r cod-smooth-coefficients}
smooth_coefs(cod_fit, select = "s(depth)")
```

## How did survey years differ?

```{r cod-year-effects, fig.alt = "Survey year contributions to log odds of encounter and log positive density, relative to 2003."}
parametric_terms(cod_fit)
year_effects <- parametric_effects(cod_fit,
  terms = c("year_f", "year_f.1"), overall_uncertainty = FALSE)
year_plot <- draw(year_effects)
year_plot[[1]] <- year_plot[[1]] +
  labs(x = "Survey year", y = "Change in log odds", subtitle = "Encounter")
year_plot[[2]] <- year_plot[[2]] +
  labs(x = "Survey year", y = "Change in log positive density",
    subtitle = "Positive density")
year_plot
```

Under the fitted treatment contrasts, 2003 is the reference year and has a
zero contribution. The other estimates are changes from that reference on
their respective link scales, after accounting for depth and fields. For the
positive-density component, exponentiating the contribution gives a ratio of
conditional mean positive density relative to 2003. For the encounter
component it gives an odds ratio, not a probability ratio. A difference in the
positive component alone is not a change in total expected density: occurrence
also matters. For example, the 2011 estimate is lower than 2003 for encounter
but higher for positive density. Looking at either component alone would miss
this distinction.

Here we requested term-only uncertainty. The reference year consequently has
no uncertainty interval for its *contrast with itself*. Request the default
`overall_uncertainty = TRUE` to include intercept uncertainty in the plotted
parametric contributions. Use full predictions to estimate actual densities.

## Did the association with depth change over survey years?

The delta model above gives each component a common depth curve and separate
year means. A different question is whether the *shape* of the depth
association changed through time. We now adapt the binomial encounter model
in sdmTMB's [introduction](https://sdmtmb.github.io/sdmTMB/articles/basic-intro.html):
replace its quadratic depth effect with a joint smooth of depth and survey
year, while retaining the spatial and independent year-specific fields and
every survey tow. This extension focuses on encounter; the delta model remains
the analysis for combined encounter and positive catch density.

A [tensor product smooth](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/t2.html)
combines bases for the two covariates and estimates smoothing for different
parts of the surface separately. This is useful when depth is measured in
metres and time in years: there is no reason to equate a metre of depth with
a year of time. The `t2()` basis has several penalties; gratia now retains
all their fitted coefficient blocks and joint uncertainty when extracting and
plotting sdmTMB effects.

```{r cod-depth-year-fit}
cod$year_centered <- cod$year - 2011
cod_encounter <- sdmTMB(
  present ~ t2(depth, year_centered, k = c(5, 4)),
  data = cod, mesh = cod_mesh, time = "year", family = binomial(),
  spatial = "on", spatiotemporal = "iid"
)
sanity(cod_encounter)
```

The joint smooth allows a gradual relationship across actual elapsed years.
The year-specific fields still represent geographical departures in each
survey, with no correlation assumed between those fields. A smooth temporal
relationship in the mean and correlation between random fields are different
assumptions. Here the smooth includes both depth and year main effects, so
we do not add the previous `year_f` factor. Centring year at 2011 only changes
its coordinate origin.

In this example the optimizer converges and the Hessian is positive definite,
but `sanity()` flags large standard errors for smoothing parameters. Inspect
the estimated standard deviations controlling the tensor penalties:

```{r cod-tensor-penalties}
sdmTMB::tidy(cod_encounter, effects = "ran_pars") |>
  filter(grepl("sd__", term)) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)
```

Two standard deviations are close to zero and their intervals are uninformative.
Some directions of curvature are being strongly penalised, and these data
weakly identify the corresponding smoothing parameters. If changes in the
depth relationship are secondary to the main survey question, the simpler
common-depth-curve model above provides a useful starting point.

```{r cod-tensor-surface, fig.alt = "Tensor smooth contribution to encounter log odds over depth and survey year. Contours are almost vertical, with unsupported deep-water combinations masked."}
tensor_panel <- draw(cod_encounter, n_2d = 30, dist = 0.1,
  wrap = FALSE)[[1]]
tensor_panel +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(-8, -4, 0, 4, 6),
    labels = c(2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2017)) +
  labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Survey year") +
  guides(fill = guide_colourbar(title = "Log-odds\ncontribution"))
```

The mostly vertical contours indicate that depth dominates the displayed
association; the preferred intermediate-depth region changes little through
time. The surface is a contribution to log odds, without the intercept or
fields. Its colours show fitted contributions; standard errors are available
from `smooth_estimates()`. `dist = 0.1` masks combinations far from the observed
depth-year pairs after scaling both covariates to a unit square. The nearly
stable intermediate-depth region is the main pattern here. The smoothing
warning and sparse deep-water observations limit the temporal changes we can
resolve in the tails.

For custom calculations, `get_smooths_by_id()` retrieves the fitted mgcv smooth
object. Its penalty list records the independently smoothed parts of the
surface; `smooth_coefs()` retrieves the corresponding coefficient vector:

```{r cod-tensor-extraction}
encounter_smooth <- get_smooths_by_id(cod_encounter, id = 1)[[1]]
length(encounter_smooth$S)
length(smooth_coefs(cod_encounter, select = smooths(cod_encounter)[1]))
```

The three penalties control different parts of one fitted surface, represented
here by nineteen coefficients. Use
`smooth_estimates(cod_encounter, data = ...)` to evaluate that surface and its
standard errors at specific depth-year combinations before carrying the
results into another calculation.

## Map expected density with full predictions

Full predictions require both components and the fields. Use sdmTMB's public
[prediction method](https://sdmtmb.github.io/sdmTMB/reference/predict.sdmTMB.html)
for this calculation. For a standard delta-Gamma model we can independently
verify the response mean from the two link-scale predictors:

```{r cod-prediction-components}
link_prediction <- predict(cod_fit)
response_prediction <- predict(cod_fit, type = "response")
combined_mean <- plogis(link_prediction$est1) * exp(link_prediction$est2)
max(abs(combined_mean - response_prediction$est))
```

For other delta links, use the fitting package's response transformation; this
product of inverse links does not apply unchanged to a coupled Poisson-link
delta model.

For mapping, use the supplied survey-area grid. Restricting the display to 2011
and 2017 keeps the figure readable; the fit still uses every survey year.

```{r cod-density-map, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Estimated expected Pacific cod density on the survey-area grid in 2011 and 2017, including fitted spatial and year-specific fields."}
map_data <- replicate_df(qcs_grid, "year", c(2011L, 2017L))
map_data$year_f <- factor(map_data$year, levels = levels(cod$year_f))
cod_map <- predict(cod_fit, newdata = map_data, type = "response")
ggplot(cod_map, aes(X, Y, fill = est)) +
  geom_raster() +
  facet_wrap(~year) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(transform = "sqrt") +
  labs(x = "Easting (km)", y = "Northing (km)",
    fill = "Mean density\n(kg/km²)")
```

The map combines encounter probability, positive density and geographical
variation. A location can have low expected density through either a low
encounter probability or a low positive mean. The maps show fitted mean
surfaces. sdmTMB's `predict(..., nsim = ...)` supplies joint prediction draws
for estimating uncertainty at each location or in derived quantities.
Setting `re_form = NA` removes spatial fields from predictions. That is a
prediction with zero fields, not an average over new fields; the nonlinear
links make these different calculations.

## What should be held fixed when checking the model?

The depth effects above omit fields from the displayed contribution, but
residual checks must use the whole fitted predictor. The sdmTMB
[residual-checking article](https://sdmtmb.github.io/sdmTMB/articles/residual-checking.html)
demonstrates why the choice of fields matters. gratia's default follows its
approach of drawing the fitted effects once from their approximate joint
posterior, with fixed coefficients and covariance parameters held at their
estimates. The observed residuals and reference responses use that same draw.

```{r cod-field-seeds}
cod_field_options <- options(gratia.diagnostics.field_seed = 1402L)
qq_plot(cod_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 1404)
```

The PIT calculation randomises zeros over their fitted probability mass, then
transforms probabilities to normal scores for this QQ plot. Given the selected
fields, response errors are independent, so the reference is standard normal
and its bands condition on those fields. A departure can indicate problems
with the observation distribution or predictor. It is not a calibrated test
of the estimated field covariance. Here, the upper tail rises above the
reference: some positive catches are larger than this fitted response
distribution anticipates. This motivates checking the positive component and
considering, for example, a delta-lognormal model, whose positive tail differs
from the Gamma distribution. Fit that alternative and repeat the positive-tail
checks to assess whether it represents the large catches better. Repeat with
other `field_seed` values to
see whether a feature of the plot depends on one fitted-field draw; the
`seed` argument separately controls randomisation at the zeros.

Examine geographical patterns as well as the pooled residual distribution:

```{r cod-residual-map, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Randomised quantile residuals at Pacific cod survey tow locations, separated by year."}
cod_residuals <- cod
cod_residuals$residual <- quantile_residuals(cod_fit,
  type = "quantile", seed = 1404)
ggplot(cod_residuals, aes(X, Y, colour = residual)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol = 4) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_colour_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red") +
  labs(x = "Easting (km)", y = "Northing (km)",
    colour = "Quantile\nresidual")
```

Clusters of residuals with the same sign deserve attention even if a QQ plot
looks acceptable. Consider omitted spatial covariates, inadequate field
resolution, or a response distribution that cannot represent the local
variation. Use geographical distances to investigate these patterns:
observation-order lags do not describe how far apart the survey tows are.

Three further choices answer different questions:

| Choice | What varies between reference data sets? | Useful interpretation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `field_method = "mle-eb"` | Response errors; estimated fields are fixed | Inspect errors at estimated fields, with shrinkage affecting calibration |
| `field_method = "mle-mvn-integrated"` | Response errors and approximate uncertainty in fitted effects | Check variation around the inferred fields, averaged across their uncertainty |
| `conditioning = "marginal"` | Response errors and new spatial and year fields from the fitted field distribution | Check the variation implied by new field realisations |

The default `field_method = "mle-mvn"` draws fitted effects once and then fixes
them; it is different from all three. Empirical-Bayes (`mle-eb`) residuals can
look too concentrated because fields were estimated from these same responses.
sdmTMB does not recommend them for goodness-of-fit testing.

```{r cod-other-field-checks, fig.height = 7}
cod_reference_options <- options(gratia.diagnostics.marginal_draws = 49L,
  gratia.diagnostics.marginal_seed = 1403L)
qq_plot(cod_fit, type = "quantile", field_method = "mle-eb", seed = 1404)
qq_plot(cod_fit, type = "quantile",
  field_method = "mle-mvn-integrated", n_simulate = 49, seed = 1404)
qq_plot(cod_fit, type = "quantile", conditioning = "marginal",
  n_simulate = 49, seed = 1404)
```

The integrated and marginal calculations use ranks in joint response
simulations. The former includes approximate uncertainty in fitted latent
effects (including penalised smooth coefficients), while holding fixed
coefficients and covariance parameters at their estimates. The latter
simulates new native spatial and temporal effects, retaining fitted smooths.
Changing `field_method` does not add another fitted-field draw to a marginal
check. These responses share field contributions, so gratia generates the
reference bands from complete simulated data sets that preserve dependence.
Independent uniform order-statistic bands would answer the wrong question.

Compare the captions as well as the curves: each plot identifies its
conditioning. In this example the integrated QQ plot describes errors around
estimated survey fields, whereas the marginal plot also reflects the wide
variation in density between possible geographical surfaces. The integrated
plot has narrower residual spread. Because integration reuses the fitting data,
apparent agreement in that plot can be conservative.
With 49 reference draws, tail resolution and Monte Carlo accuracy are limited.
Increase `gratia.diagnostics.marginal_draws` and `n_simulate` to check that a
conclusion persists; the defaults use more reference draws.

## Is a problem in occurrence or in positive density?

Component checks help locate a mismatch hidden in a full-response check.
For the positive component, only observed positive tows are retained; the
binomial component retains the complete presence/absence sample.

```{r cod-component-checks, fig.height = 7}
qq_plot(cod_fit, type = "quantile", component = "positive", seed = 1404)
posterior_predictive_plot(cod_fit, component = "binomial",
  n = 25, seed = 1405)
```

The occurrence plot compares the observed proportions at 0 and 1 with
replicated proportions. Its intervals describe variation across posterior
replicates, including parameter and fitted-field uncertainty. These are not
the intervals for independent proportions from a binomial sample. A good
aggregate proportion can conceal geographical mismatch, so retain the spatial
residual map and inspect component maps if necessary.

Unlike residual references with coefficients fixed at their estimates,
posterior predictive checks draw fixed coefficients, nuisance parameters,
smooth coefficients and fields together from the approximate joint
posterior. Conditional checks draw uncertain *fitted* fields; marginal checks
replace these with *new* fields at each parameter draw. `field_method` selects
residual calculations and is not an option for PPCs.

For the complete density distribution, smoothing a kernel density curve over
an exact-zero spike is hard to interpret. Raw public `posterior_samples()`
allow a targeted comparison of zero frequency and a positive-tail summary:

```{r cod-posterior-summaries}
cod_summaries <- function(x) {
  c(proportion_zero = mean(x == 0), density_95th = unname(quantile(x, 0.95)))
}
observed_summary <- cod_summaries(cod$density)
conditional_draws <- posterior_samples(cod_fit, n_draws = 25, seed = 1405)
marginal_draws <- posterior_samples(cod_fit, n_draws = 25,
  conditioning = "marginal", seed = 1405)

summarise_draws <- function(x, description) {
  x |>
    group_by(.draw) |>
    summarise(proportion_zero = mean(.response == 0),
      density_95th = quantile(.response, 0.95), .groups = "drop") |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-.draw, names_to = "summary", values_to = "value") |>
    mutate(check = description)
}
summary_draws <- bind_rows(
  summarise_draws(conditional_draws, "Uncertain fitted fields"),
  summarise_draws(marginal_draws, "New fields")
)
observed_table <- data.frame(summary = names(observed_summary),
  observed = unname(observed_summary))
summary_draws |>
  group_by(check, summary) |>
  summarise(median = median(value), lower = quantile(value, 0.05),
    upper = quantile(value, 0.95), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(observed_table, by = "summary")
```

The conditional comparison asks whether new responses around the inferred
survey fields reproduce these summaries. The marginal comparison asks whether
new field realisations at the survey locations reproduce them. About 54% of
observed tows are zero, and the observed 95th percentile is about 157 kg/km².
Both fall within the displayed predictive ranges. This agrees with reproducing
these aggregate summaries, while the conditional QQ plot still flags the
more extreme positive tail. Passing a check of the 95th percentile does not
establish that the largest catches are well represented. Wider marginal
variation is scientifically plausible because these summaries change when a
large part of the area happens to have high or low density. The displayed
intervals are descriptive 90% predictive ranges from just 25 replicates.
Increase the draw count before interpreting an apparent tail discrepancy.
These summaries describe the sampling locations; an area-standardised biomass
index requires predictions across the survey domain.

## Breakpoint and logistic curves

sdmTMB also offers two structured alternatives to a smooth. `breakpt(x)` fits
a line up to an estimated breakpoint and a constant beyond it. `logistic(x)`
fits a sigmoid curve. gratia draws these as parametric effects, with one
curve for each component of a delta model. The argument of either term must
name a column in the fitting data, following sdmTMB's formula restrictions.

A small simulated example shows both shapes without refitting the survey
model. Starting values place the breakpoint within the observed range and
give the logistic curve a positive distance between its 50% and 95% locations.
sdmTMB stores the logarithm of this distance as the second logistic parameter.

```{r fit-threshold-curves}
set.seed(312)
threshold_data <- data.frame(x = runif(400, 0, 2))
threshold_data$breakpt_y <- 0.4 + 1.8 * pmin(threshold_data$x, 0.9) +
  rnorm(nrow(threshold_data), sd = 0.15)
threshold_data$logistic_y <- 0.4 +
  2.2 * plogis(log(19) * (threshold_data$x - 0.8) / 0.6) +
  rnorm(nrow(threshold_data), sd = 0.15)
breakpt_fit <- sdmTMB(
  breakpt_y ~ breakpt(x), data = threshold_data, spatial = "off",
  control = sdmTMBcontrol(backend = "rtmb",
    start = list(b_threshold = matrix(c(1.5, 0.8), ncol = 1)))
)
logistic_fit <- sdmTMB(
  logistic_y ~ logistic(x), data = threshold_data, spatial = "off",
  control = sdmTMBcontrol(backend = "rtmb",
    start = list(b_threshold = matrix(c(0.8, log(0.6), 2), ncol = 1)))
)
sanity(breakpt_fit)
sanity(logistic_fit)
```

Select these curves using `terms`, as for the survey-year effects above.
`parametric_terms()` lists their labels. In a delta model, `breakpt(x).1` or
`logistic(x).1` selects the second component. `parametric = FALSE` suppresses
threshold curves; selecting smooths with `select` excludes parametric effects
unless `parametric = TRUE` is also supplied.

```{r threshold-curves, fig.alt = "Estimated breakpoint and logistic contributions, with pointwise uncertainty bands and rugs."}
parametric_terms(breakpt_fit)
parametric_terms(logistic_fit)
threshold_panels <- c(
  draw(breakpt_fit, terms = "breakpt(x)", n = 100, wrap = FALSE),
  assemble(logistic_fit, terms = "logistic(x)", n = 100)
)
wrap_plots(threshold_panels, ncol = 2)
```

Each curve is its uncentred contribution to the linear predictor. The
intercept is not added to that contribution. The bands use pointwise
delta-method standard errors from the joint covariance of the fitted
threshold parameters. By default, they also include the intercept's
uncertainty and its covariance with those parameters. Use
`overall_uncertainty = FALSE` for uncertainty in the threshold contribution
alone. Threshold bands remain pointwise when `interval = "simultaneous"`
is requested for smooths in the same model.

The default evaluation grid contains `n` equally spaced values over the
fitted covariate range. For a breakpoint curve, it also contains the fitted
breakpoint when that lies within the range, so the plotted line changes slope
at the fitted location. Supply `data` to choose evaluation locations instead.
Rugs continue to show fitting observations. The threshold covariate is
already on its original scale, so `back_transform` does not change its axis.
`constant` shifts the curve and interval together; `fun` then transforms both.

```{r threshold-values}
parametric_effects(logistic_fit, terms = "logistic(x)",
  data = data.frame(x = c(0.25, 0.75, 1.25)),
  overall_uncertainty = FALSE)
```

## Coefficients that vary through time

A covariate's coefficient can change through time in sdmTMB. For example,
temperature may have a stronger association with abundance in some years
than in others. The `time_varying` formula specifies which coefficients
vary, while `time_varying_type` defines the process connecting successive
values. `~ 1` varies the intercept; `~ 0 + temperature` varies just the
temperature coefficient; `~ temperature` varies both.

The three processes differ in how they represent the coefficient's level:

* `"rw"` estimates the first coefficient freely and penalises changes
  between time steps. Omit its corresponding ordinary term from the main
  formula. If the intercept varies, omit the main formula's intercept too.
* `"rw0"` estimates deviations whose first value is shrunk towards zero,
  followed by a random walk. Include an ordinary coefficient for the baseline.
* `"ar1"` estimates correlated deviations around zero. Include an ordinary
  coefficient for the average effect.

This simulated example fits all three specifications to the same data. The
temperature coefficient changes over 20 years, with 35 observations per year.
Spatial and spatiotemporal fields are switched off so that the example focuses
on the changing coefficient.

```{r fit-time-varying-coefficients}
set.seed(420)
coefficient_years <- 2005:2024
temperature_coefficient <- 0.8 +
  as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.72), n = length(coefficient_years), sd = 0.13))
coefficient_data <- data.frame(
  year = rep(coefficient_years, each = 35),
  temperature = rnorm(length(coefficient_years) * 35)
)
coefficient_data$response <- 0.6 +
  rep(temperature_coefficient, each = 35) * coefficient_data$temperature +
  rnorm(nrow(coefficient_data), sd = 0.65)
coefficient_fits <- lapply(c("rw", "rw0", "ar1"), function(process) {
  main_formula <- if (process == "rw") response ~ 1 else response ~ temperature
  sdmTMB(
    main_formula, data = coefficient_data, time = "year",
    time_varying = ~ 0 + temperature, time_varying_type = process,
    spatial = "off", spatiotemporal = "off",
    control = sdmTMBcontrol(backend = "rtmb")
  )
})
names(coefficient_fits) <- c("rw", "rw0", "ar1")
lapply(coefficient_fits, sanity)
```

`draw()` plots the full coefficient over time: the fitted trajectory for
`rw`, or the ordinary coefficient plus its temporal deviation for `rw0`
and `ar1`. Points mark the modelled time steps, straight lines connect
them, and a ribbon shows the pointwise interval. The following panels are
ordered `rw`, `rw0` and `ar1`.

```{r time-varying-coefficient-ribbons, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Full temperature coefficient trajectories from rw, rw0 and ar1 models, with points at each year and uncertainty ribbons."}
coefficient_panels <- lapply(coefficient_fits, function(fit) {
  assemble(fit, terms = "time_varying(temperature)")[[1L]]
})
wrap_plots(coefficient_panels, ncol = 3)
```

Use `time_varying_style = "pointrange"` to show interval bars at each time
step. This also works when drawing saved estimates.

```{r time-varying-coefficient-intervals, fig.alt = "Full temperature coefficients from the AR1 model, with pointwise interval bars and a connecting line."}
coefficient_estimates <- parametric_effects(coefficient_fits$ar1,
  terms = "time_varying(temperature)")
draw(coefficient_estimates, time_varying_style = "pointrange")
```

For a coefficient written as $b_t = \beta + \gamma_t$, the variance is

\[
\operatorname{Var}(b_t) = \operatorname{Var}(\beta) +
  \operatorname{Var}(\gamma_t) + 2\operatorname{Cov}(\beta, \gamma_t).
\]

gratia uses this joint covariance when combining the ordinary coefficient
and temporal deviations. A slope's interval includes uncertainty in that
slope's ordinary coefficient, without adding uncertainty from a separate
response intercept. `overall_uncertainty` continues to control ordinary
partial effects; time-varying panels always retain the full coefficient's
uncertainty. These intervals remain pointwise when simultaneous bands are
requested for smooths in the same model. `ci_level` changes their coverage;
`constant` shifts estimates and intervals together, then `fun` transforms both.

`parametric_terms()` lists the available labels. Use
`time_varying(Intercept)` for a varying intercept, and append `.1` to select
a trajectory in the second delta component. Each fitted coefficient gets
its own panel, including separate factor contrasts, transformed variables
and interaction coefficients. The ordinary and time-varying design columns
must have compatible coding when the corresponding ordinary term is present.
An absent ordinary coefficient contributes zero to the full coefficient.

By default, the ordinary-effect panel is omitted when its coefficients are
included in a trajectory. Request its original selector explicitly to draw
it, for example `draw(coefficient_fits$ar1, terms = "temperature")`.
`parametric = FALSE` suppresses trajectories; selecting smooths with
`select` excludes them unless `parametric = TRUE` is also supplied.

The estimates use the stored modelled time steps, including `extra_time`
values supplied when fitting. `n` does not create additional coefficient
states. The stored time spacing is retained. A `data` frame containing the
time column selects stored times; missing or unknown requested times give an
error. If `data` has no
time column, the complete trajectory is retained.

```{r time-varying-coefficient-selection}
parametric_terms(coefficient_fits$ar1)
parametric_effects(coefficient_fits$ar1,
  terms = "time_varying(temperature)",
  data = data.frame(year = c(2005, 2010, 2020)))
```

## Applying the workflow to another survey

Retain the scientific unit of the response and its zeros when selecting a
family. Consider whether encounter and positive-density processes need
separate predictors, and justify temporal dependence from the survey schedule.
Check convergence before interpreting partial effects. Use effect plots for
formula contributions and full fitting-package predictions for maps and
indices. Match each diagnostic to whether the scientific question concerns
the observed fields or new fields, and examine spatial patterns alongside
marginal distribution plots.

The support has deliberate limits. gratia does not supply partial residual
overlays or random-field effect plots for sdmTMB. Formula-effect extraction
does not cover dispersion formulas, other multi-predictor families,
or nonlocal effects. It cannot use mapped or profiled coefficients needed for
extraction, unavailable smooth metadata, or a covariance from a
non-positive-definite Hessian. `unconditional = TRUE` and `frequentist = TRUE`
are mgcv covariance choices and do not apply to these joint RTMB intervals.
Use sdmTMB's prediction and plotting methods for fields and unsupported
formula effects. If the covariance is unavailable, investigate convergence
before interpreting intervals. Diagnostic families and additional limits
are listed in `?diagnostic_support`.

```{r restore-options, include = FALSE}
options(cod_field_options)
options(cod_reference_options)
```
